comm.t: Medhas resumes for King Suratha and the merchant Samādhi. Niśumbha has fallen at the end of chapter 9; this chapter tells the last duel, between the Goddess and Śumbha, and closes the third story (Uttama Carita, chapters 5–13).

In the Gita Press pāṭha the chapter is preceded by its own dhyāna, which meditates on the Goddess as Kāmeśvarī, ‘the form of Śiva and Śakti’ (शिवशक्तिरूपां कामेश्वरीं). The dhyāna and the bīja ॐ that opens this mantra in recitation belong to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa.

mantras.tr: When Śumbha saw his brother Niśumbha, dear to him as life, lying slain, and his army being cut down, he spoke in fury.

comm.t: The link from chapter 9: Niśumbha is dead and the remaining army is being destroyed. Śumbha, now alone, addresses the Goddess directly.
A modern reading: the text gives the demon a human grief — the brother was ‘equal to his life’. The anger that follows grows out of loss as well as pride.

mantras.anvaya: दुष्टे दुर्गे, त्वं बलावलेपात् गर्वं मा आवह। या (त्वम्) अतिमानिनी (असि, सा त्वम्) अन्यासां बलम् आश्रित्य युद्ध्यसे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: a prohibition (मा … आवह) with a causal ablative, and an accusation whose subject is the relative या … अतिमानिनी (‘you, who are so proud’).
mantras.lit: O wicked Durgā, do not carry pride out of the arrogance of strength. You who are exceedingly proud fight relying on the strength of other (women).
mantras.tr: Wicked Durgā, do not swell with pride in your power! For all your arrogance, you fight leaning on the strength of others.
mantras.tr_note: या अतिमानिनी, literally ‘(you) who (are) exceedingly proud’, is rendered ‘for all your arrogance’.

comm.t: Śumbha’s taunt: the Goddess has not fought alone. The Mothers (Brahmāṇī and the others, 8.13 ff.) and Śivadūtī fought beside her in chapters 8–9, and Śumbha himself came to the field after they had fought (9.8). He calls this borrowed strength.
The charge prepares the answer of 10.5: what Śumbha sees as ‘others’ is the Goddess herself. The tradition reads the taunt as the demon’s error in its purest form — he sees many where there is one.
A modern reading: Śumbha’s accusation is the one we make of anyone whose strength we cannot explain — that it must come from somewhere else.

mantras.anvaya: अत्र जगति अहम् एका एव (अस्मि)। मम अपरा द्वितीया का (अस्ति)? दुष्ट, पश्य — एताः मद्विभूतयः मयि एव विशन्त्यः (सन्ति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A statement (एका एव अहम्), a rhetorical question (द्वितीया का मम अपरा), and an imperative introducing a nominal clause (पश्य — एताः … विशन्त्यः मद्विभूतयः).
mantras.lit: I am alone, one only, here in the world. What second, other than me, is there? O wicked one, look: these, my powers, are entering into me alone.
mantras.tr: I am alone in this world. Who else is there besides me? See, wicked one: these powers of mine are entering into me.

comm.t: The Goddess answers the charge of 10.3. The ‘others’ (अन्यासाम्) are not others: they are her own vibhūtis, and as she speaks they merge back into her (10.6). Śumbha has been fighting her all along.

In the Śākta tradition this verse is a central statement of the text’s non-dualism: the many goddesses are one Goddess, and the world holds no second power beside her. The narrative first called them the śaktis of the gods, come out of the gods’ bodies (8.13); here the Goddess claims them as her own, and the Kaumārī of 8.17 is already called ‘Ambikā in the form of Guha’ (अम्बिका गुहरूपिणी).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has names that state the same idea: एकाकिनी (665, ‘the one who is alone’), निर्द्वैता (667) and द्वैतवर्जिता (668, ‘free of duality’). The hymns are separate works; the shared doctrine is common Śākta thought.

A modern reading: there is an echo of Śumbha’s own message in 5.111, which claimed that every jewel among gods, gandharvas and serpents rests ‘in me alone’ (मय्येव). The Goddess uses the same words truthfully: what seemed to be many is gathered into one.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the goddesses (subject, with three qualifiers) ‘go to dissolution’ in her body; then Ambikā is alone.
mantras.lit: Then all those goddesses, headed by Brahmāṇī, went to absorption in the body of that Goddess. Then Ambikā was alone, one only.
mantras.tr: Then all those goddesses, Brahmāṇī and the rest, dissolved into the Goddess’s body, and Ambikā stood alone.

comm.t: The narrator confirms in action what the Goddess has just said (10.5): the Mothers enter her body and vanish. The verse repeats her own word, एका एव, of the Goddess as she now stands.
लय is also the word for the world’s dissolution (pralaya). Read in that light in the Śākta tradition, the powers are not dismissed but resolved into their source.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls the Goddess लयकरी (739), ‘she who brings about dissolution’. The name is general; here the dissolution is of her own manifested forms.

morph.note: Two constructions are possible. (1) Relative pronoun, object of आस्थिता: ‘that (state) which I had assumed here in many forms … that is withdrawn’, with तत् as its correlative — taken here. (2) Adverbial यत् = यदा, ‘when I stood here in many forms … that was withdrawn’; then तत् refers to the plurality itself. The sense is the same.
आ + √स्था ‘to take one’s stand on, assume’ is transitive; its past participle can be active in sense and take an object (यत्): ‘(I) who had assumed’.
सम् + √हृ ‘to draw together, withdraw’ — the same verb that names the dissolution of the world (saṃhāra). मया is its agent.
√स्था forms its present stem by reduplication (ष्ठा → तिष्ठ-), listed with the bhvādi class.

mantras.anvaya: अहं विभूत्या इह बहुभिः रूपैः यत् आस्थिता, तत् मया संहृतम्। (अधुना) एका एव आजौ तिष्ठामि। स्थिरः भव।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative-correlative sentence (यत् … आस्थिता, तत् … संहृतम्), a statement (एका एव तिष्ठामि) and an imperative (स्थिरः भव).
mantras.lit: What I had assumed here, through my power of manifestation, in many forms — that has been withdrawn by me. I stand alone in battle. Be steady!
mantras.tr: Through my power I stood here in many forms; those I have withdrawn. Now I stand alone on the battlefield — stand firm!
mantras.tr_note: The tr follows the reading यत् = ‘what (state)’, simplified to ‘those (forms) I have withdrawn’; ‘now’ is supplied.

comm.t: The Goddess explains what Śumbha has seen: the many forms were her own power (विभूति) displayed; she has withdrawn them, and now meets him alone. स्थिरो भव is a challenge: ‘hold your ground’.

The verb संहृतम् belongs to the vocabulary of cosmic dissolution (saṃhāra), and in the Śākta tradition the verse is read in that light: what the Goddess projects she can take back, and the manifold is her own, not another’s. The word विभूति is the one the Bhagavad Gītā uses for the divine manifestations in its tenth chapter.
A modern reading: the Goddess answers the charge of dependence not by argument but by demonstration — she withdraws every helper and stays.

mantras.tr: Then, as all the gods and the asuras looked on, a terrible battle began between the two, the Goddess and Śumbha.

A modern reading: the genitive absolute (पश्यताम्) makes both worlds witnesses. The last battle is fought in the open, before gods and asuras alike, so that its outcome cannot be disputed.

mantras.anvaya_en: Instruments (शरवर्षैः, शस्त्रैः, अस्त्रैः, each with its adjective), the genitive तयोः, and the main clause युद्धं भूयः अभूत् with the predicate adjective सर्वलोकभयङ्करम्.
mantras.lit: With showers of arrows, with sharp weapons, and likewise with terrible missiles too, the battle of the two took place again, causing fear to all the worlds.
mantras.tr: With volleys of arrows, keen-edged weapons and fearsome missiles the battle between them raged on, terrifying all the worlds.

comm.t: The duel is fought first with weapons at a distance. The pair शस्त्र / अस्त्र is the usual Epic distinction: weapons held in the hand and missiles that are thrown or charged with power (the divine astras of the next verse). For the second half of the first line other witnesses read तथा चास्त्रैः सुदारुणैः (GRETIL, Freund) for the Gita Press तथास्त्रैश्चैव दारुणैः; the sense, ‘and with (very) terrible missiles’, is the same. The Gita Press reading is kept.

mantras.anvaya: अथ अम्बिका यानि दिव्यानि अस्त्राणि शतशः मुमुचे, तानि दैत्येन्द्रः तत्प्रतीघातकर्तृभिः (अस्त्रैः) बभञ्ज।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यानि … मुमुचे) names the object; the main clause (तानि … बभञ्ज) has its instrument in तत्प्रतीघातकर्तृभिः.
mantras.lit: The divine missiles which Ambikā then released by hundreds — those the lord of the Daityas shattered with (weapons) that effect the counter-blow to them.
mantras.tr: The divine missiles Ambikā loosed by the hundred, the Daitya king shattered with counter-weapons.

comm.t: The first exchange: the Goddess’s divine astras are met and broken by Śumbha’s counter-weapons. He is a worthy opponent; the narrative does not make the victory easy.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) describes the same kind of duel in its own war story, naming the Goddess भण्डासुरेन्द्रनिर्मुक्तशस्त्रप्रत्यस्त्रवर्षिणी (79), ‘she who rains counter-weapons against the weapons released by Bhaṇḍāsura’. There it is the Goddess who counters; here, for a moment, it is the demon.

mantras.anvaya: परमेश्वरी च तेन मुक्तानि दिव्यानि अस्त्राणि उग्रहुङ्कारोच्चारणादिभिः लीलया एव बभञ्ज।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject परमेश्वरी, verb बभञ्ज, object अस्त्राणि with two qualifiers (मुक्तानि तेन, दिव्यानि), and two instrumentals: लीलया (manner) and उग्रहुङ्कारोच्चारणादिभिः (means).
mantras.lit: And the supreme Sovereign broke the divine missiles released by him, just in play, with utterances of a fierce ‘hum’ and the like.
mantras.tr: And the divine missiles he released, the supreme Goddess broke as if in play, with a fierce cry of ‘hum’ and other such means.

comm.t: The Goddess’s answer to 10.12: where Śumbha needed counter-weapons, she needs only a sound. The हुङ्कार has done this before — it laid low Mahiṣa’s spear (3.12) and burned Dhūmralocana to ashes (6.13).
In the Śākta tradition the hum-sound is the Goddess’s own power of speech used as a weapon; the verse sets lordship (परमेश्वरी) beside play (लीलया): the supreme ruler acts without effort.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names her परमेश्वरी (396), and calls her लीलाविनोदिनी (966), ‘she who delights in play’. The names express a shared Śākta idea; the texts are separate.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: Śumbha’s attack (शरशतैः … आच्छादयत) and the Goddess’s reply (सा … धनुः च चिच्छेद इषुभिः). च here joins the clauses; the possessive ‘his’ is supplied.
mantras.lit: Then that asura covered the Goddess with hundreds of arrows. She too, the Goddess, angered at that, cut his bow with arrows.
mantras.tr: Then the asura covered the Goddess with arrows by the hundred; and she, angered, cut his bow apart with her own arrows.

comm.t: Śumbha tries to overwhelm her with sheer numbers; the Goddess answers by cutting his bow. The sequence of 10.14–19 strips him of each weapon in turn: bow, spear, sword and shield, chariot, mace.
A modern reading: the Goddess does not answer numbers with numbers. She removes the means of attack, one at a time.

mantras.lit: The bow having been cut, the lord of the Daityas then took up a spear. The Goddess cut that too, resting in his hand, with her discus.
mantras.tr: His bow cut through, the Daitya lord seized a spear; that too the Goddess cut with her discus while it was still in his hand.
mantras.tr_note: ‘while it was still in his hand’ renders अस्य करे स्थिताम्, ‘resting in his hand’.

comm.t: The second weapon goes: the spear (शक्ति) is cut before it can be thrown — while it is still ‘resting in his hand’.
A modern reading: the word शक्ति is used here of the demon’s weapon. The narrative lets ‘power’ in his hand be cut by the one who is Power itself — an irony the Sanskrit permits but does not state.

mantras.lit: Then, taking up a sword and a shining shield marked with a hundred moons, the lord of the Daityas’ chiefs then rushed at the Goddess.
mantras.tr: Then the overlord of the Daityas took up a sword and a gleaming shield adorned with a hundred moons, and charged at the Goddess.
mantras.tr_note: ततः and तदा both mean ‘then’; the second is not repeated in tr.

comm.t: With bow and spear gone, Śumbha closes in with sword and shield. शतचन्द्र, ‘hundred-moon’, is the Epic name for a shield decorated with moon-shaped ornaments; भानुमत् ‘shining’ describes it.

For अभ्यधावत्तदा देवीं other witnesses read अभ्यधावत तां देवीं (GRETIL, Freund): the middle form of the verb with the pronoun ताम् instead of the adverb तदा. The meaning is unchanged; the Gita Press reading is kept.

mantras.anvaya: आपततः एव तस्य खड्गं चण्डिका आशु चिच्छेद, धनुर्मुक्तैः शितैः बाणैः अर्ककरामलं चर्म च (चिच्छेद)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject चण्डिका, verb चिच्छेद with two objects: खड्गम् (with तस्य आपततः एव and आशु) and चर्म (with its instrument बाणैः and qualifier).
mantras.lit: Even as he was rushing on, Caṇḍikā swiftly cut his sword, and with sharp arrows shot from the bow (she cut) his shield, spotless as the sun’s rays.
mantras.tr: As he rushed in, Caṇḍikā swiftly cut his sword in two, and with keen arrows from her bow she split his shield, bright as sunlight.

comm.t: Sword and shield go together. The first half-line is the formula already used for Niśumbha in 9.33 (तस्यापतत एवाशु गदां चिच्छेद चण्डिका, there with the club): the Goddess strikes before the blow can land.

Other witnesses (GRETIL, Freund) add a third line here: अश्वांश्च पातयामास रथं सारथिना सह, ‘and she brought down his horses, and the chariot with the charioteer’. It is not in the Gita Press text, whose colophon count (27 ślokas and one half-śloka) agrees with the two-line form. The line would explain the next verse, where Śumbha is suddenly ‘horseless’ and ‘charioteerless’.

mantras.lit: Then that Daitya — horses slain, bow cut, without charioteer — intent on the death of Ambikā, seized a dreadful mace.
mantras.tr: Then the Daitya, his horses killed, his bow cut, his charioteer gone, still bent on killing Ambikā, seized a dreadful mace.

comm.t: Śumbha has lost chariot horses, bow and charioteer; he fights on, now on foot, with a mace. In the Gita Press text the loss of horses and charioteer is stated only here, by the compounds; the extra line found in other witnesses at 10.17 narrates it.
A modern reading: three compounds strip the king, one loss at a time — yet the last compound is his unchanged intent (अम्बिकानिधनोद्यतः). Nothing that is taken from him alters his purpose.

mantras.lit: (She) cut, with sharpened arrows, the mace of him as he was rushing on. Even so he, impetuous, raising his fist, rushed at her.
mantras.tr: As he charged, she cut his mace apart with keen arrows; even so he rushed at her, fist raised, in his fury.

comm.t: The last weapon is gone; Śumbha attacks with his bare fist. The pattern of 10.17 is repeated: the weapon is cut ‘as he rushes on’, before the blow.
A modern reading: the text gives the demon no surrender. The narrative of 10.14–19 removes every instrument he has, and he keeps coming with his hands.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: Śumbha’s blow (सः … मुष्टिं पातयामास, with हृदये देव्याः) and the Goddess’s (सा देवी … तम् उरसि अताडयत्). देव्याः, printed at the head of the second line, belongs with हृदये in the first clause.
mantras.lit: He, the bull among the Daityas, brought down his fist on the heart of the Goddess. And she, the Goddess, in turn struck him on the chest with her palm.
mantras.tr: The mightiest of the Daityas brought his fist down on the Goddess’s heart; and she in turn struck him on the chest with the flat of her hand.

comm.t: Śumbha’s fist reaches the Goddess’s heart. Her answer is an open-handed blow (तलेन) to his chest, which fells him (10.21).
A modern reading: fist against open palm — the narrative contrasts his clenched effort with her unclenched hand, and the open hand is the stronger.

mantras.lit: Struck by the blow of her palm, (he) fell down on the surface of the earth. That king of the Daityas at once rose up again, just so.
mantras.tr: Felled by the blow of her open hand, he crashed to the ground — and at once the Daitya king was on his feet again.

A modern reading: the narrative repeatedly lets Śumbha rise. His strength is real; what defeats him is not weakness but the One he fights.

mantras.anvaya: (सः) उत्पत्य च देवीं प्रगृह्य उच्चैः गगनम् आस्थितः। तत्र अपि सा चण्डिका निराधारा तेन युयुधे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: Śumbha (understood subject) with two absolutives (उत्पत्य, प्रगृह्य) and the participle आस्थितः; then the Goddess with युयुधे and the instrumental तेन.
mantras.lit: And having leapt up and seized the Goddess, (he) went up high into the sky. Even there Caṇḍikā, without support, fought with him.
mantras.tr: He sprang up, seized the Goddess, and rose high into the sky; and there too, with nothing to stand on, Caṇḍikā fought him.

comm.t: Śumbha carries the fight into the air. The Goddess needs no ground under her: निराधारा, ‘without a support’, she fights on in the sky.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same word as a name, निराधारा (132), where it means ‘she who depends on nothing’ — a metaphysical attribute. Here the word is literal: she fights in mid-air. The two senses meet, but the texts are separate.
A modern reading: Śumbha moves the battle off the earth, as if a change of ground could change its outcome. The Goddess, who rests on nothing, is not moved by it.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two subjects joined by च with a dual verb (चक्रतुः); the object नियुद्धम् carries two qualifiers (प्रथमम्, सिद्धमुनिविस्मयकारकम्).
mantras.lit: Then the Daitya and Caṇḍikā waged with each other in the sky a close fight, the first (of its kind), causing wonder to the siddhas and sages.
mantras.tr: There in the sky the Daitya and Caṇḍikā grappled with each other, a fight such as had never been seen, which filled the siddhas and the sages with wonder.
mantras.tr_note: प्रथमम्, ‘first (of its kind)’, is rendered ‘such as had never been seen’.

comm.t: The duel becomes a wrestling match (नियुद्ध, close combat without weapons) in the open sky, watched by the siddhas and sages.
A modern reading: at the end, all instruments are gone; the struggle is body to body. The text leaves nothing between the demon and the Goddess.

mantras.lit: Then Ambikā, having waged close combat with him for a very long time, lifted (him) up, whirled (him) round, and hurled (him) on the surface of the earth.
mantras.tr: After wrestling with him a long while, Ambikā lifted him high, whirled him round and flung him down to the earth.

comm.t: The Goddess ends the sky-fight: three verbs in sequence — lifting, whirling, hurling — bring Śumbha back to earth. The object (him) is understood throughout.
A modern reading: Śumbha had carried the Goddess into the sky (10.22); now she carries him and throws him down. The verse reverses his action exactly.

An adjective in -इत from the noun वेग, ‘one in whom speed has arisen’: rushing, impetuous.

mantras.anvaya: क्षिप्तः सः धरणीं प्राप्य वेगितः मुष्टिम् उद्यम्य दुष्टात्मा चण्डिकानिधनेच्छया अभ्यधावत।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सः (with क्षिप्तः, वेगितः, दुष्टात्मा), two absolutive phrases (धरणीं प्राप्य; मुष्टिम् उद्यम्य), an instrumental of motive, and the verb अभ्यधावत.
mantras.lit: He, thrown, having reached the earth, raising his fist, impetuous — the wicked-souled one rushed forward with the desire to kill Caṇḍikā.
mantras.tr: Hurled down, he struck the earth, then sprang at her, fist raised, the evil one, still longing to kill Caṇḍikā.

comm.t: Thrown to the ground, Śumbha attacks once more with his fist. The verse repeats the language of 10.19 (मुष्टिमुद्यम्य) and of 10.18 (the wish to kill her): his intent never changes.
A modern reading: the narrative gives the demon the same gesture three times — raising his fist. Persistence without insight is the shape of his whole story.

The same causative periphrastic perfect as in 10.20, here with the Goddess as subject: ‘made (him) fall’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देवी आयान्तं सर्वदैत्यजनेश्वरं तं शूलेन वक्षसि भित्त्वा जगत्यां पातयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject देवी, verb पातयामास, object तम् (with आयान्तम् and the epithet), the absolutive phrase शूलेन वक्षसि भित्त्वा, and the locative जगत्याम्.
mantras.lit: Then the Goddess, having pierced him in the chest with her trident, felled him, the lord of all the Daitya people, as he was coming on, upon the earth.
mantras.tr: Then, as the lord of all the Daityas came at her, the Goddess pierced his chest with her trident and struck him down to the earth.

comm.t: The death blow. After the weapons, the sky-fight and the wrestling, the Goddess ends the battle with her trident (शूल) through his chest, as she pierced Niśumbha’s heart with her trident (9.34) before beheading the figure that came out of it (9.35–36).

A modern reading: the epithet given at the moment of death — ‘lord of all the Daitya people’ — states what falls with him. The king is the last of his army; with him the whole order of the asuras ends.

samasa.literal: (the earth) that is together with mountains

Masculine nominative of the u-stem compound; असु ‘life-breath’ is used in the plural (असवः), hence गताः असवः.

mantras.anvaya: देवीशूलाग्रविक्षतः गतासुः सः साब्धिद्वीपां सपर्वतां सकलां पृथ्वीं चालयन् उर्व्यां पपात।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सः with two qualifiers (गतासुः, देवीशूलाग्रविक्षतः), verb पपात with the locative उर्व्याम्, and the participial phrase चालयन् … पृथ्वीम् with its three qualifiers.
mantras.lit: He, lifeless, wounded by the point of the Goddess’s trident, fell on the earth, shaking the whole earth with its oceans and continents, with its mountains.
mantras.tr: Pierced by the point of the Goddess’s trident, he fell lifeless to the ground, and the whole earth shook — its oceans, its continents and its mountains.

comm.t: Śumbha dies. His fall shakes the whole earth — a measure of his size and power, and of the scale of what has been overcome. With his death the battle of the third carita is over; the next chapter (11) is the gods’ hymn of thanksgiving to Nārāyaṇī.
A modern reading: the earth that the asuras had held in fear shakes one last time under their king’s body — and then, in the verses that follow, is still.

mantras.lit: Then, that evil-souled one having been slain, the whole world, become serene, attained exceeding well-being, and the sky became stainless.
mantras.tr: When that wicked one was slain, the whole world grew serene and was restored to perfect health, and the sky became clear.

comm.t: The cosmic consequence of the victory: the world (जगत्) recovers its health, and the sky clears. Verses 10.28–32 describe the return of order in nature.
A modern reading: स्वास्थ्य, ‘health’, is literally ‘being established in oneself’. The verse pictures the world, freed of oppression, returning to its own nature.

mantras.anvaya_en: A relative-correlative sentence (ये … आसन्, ते शमं ययुः) and a second sentence with a locative absolute (तत्र पातिते).
mantras.lit: The portent-clouds, with meteors, which had been before — they went to calm. When (he) had been felled there, the rivers likewise became flowing in their courses.
mantras.tr: The ominous clouds and falling meteors that had been seen before all vanished, and once he had fallen, the rivers flowed again within their banks.
mantras.tr_note: ‘within their banks’ interprets मार्गवाहिन्यः, ‘flowing by (their) course’.

comm.t: The signs of disorder disappear: the ominous clouds and meteors that had accompanied the asura reign subside, and the rivers return to their beds.

The gods will ask in their hymn (11.34) that the Goddess quell ‘the great calamities born of the ripening of portents’ (उत्पातपाकजनितान् … महोपसर्गान्). The vocabulary of portents in this verse anticipates that prayer.

Here an adverb, ‘sweetly’ (as in 7.26, ललितं … वचः); it is not a name.

mantras.lit: Then, he having been slain, all the hosts of gods became those whose minds are filled with joy; the gandharvas sang sweetly.
mantras.tr: Then, with Śumbha slain, all the hosts of the gods were filled with joy, and the gandharvas sang sweetly.

comm.t: The celebration begins. The scene repeats the rejoicing after Mahiṣa’s death (3.44: जगुर्गन्धर्वपतयो ननृतुश्चाप्सरोगणाः), as the end of each great battle is marked by music and dance.
A modern reading: the gods have not fought this last battle; they have only watched (10.10). Their joy is the joy of those who are saved by another.

mantras.lit: Likewise others played (instruments), and the troops of apsarases danced. Likewise pure winds blew; the sun became of fair radiance.
mantras.tr: Others played music, the apsarases danced, pure winds blew, and the sun shone brightly.

comm.t: The joy of heaven is matched by the healing of nature: music and dance among the gods, pure winds and a clear sun in the world.
A modern reading: the verse joins two orders of response — the arts of the celestials and the weather of the earth. Liberation is shown as both festivity and the return of ordinary health.

morph.note: The same participle twice, in two functions. The first qualifies अग्नयः: the fires blazed ‘calm’ — burning steadily rather than flaring (alt.: ‘the fires that had been quenched blazed up again’, शान्ताः then meaning ‘extinguished’). The second is the predicate of the next clause: ‘stilled (were) the sounds’.

mantras.anvaya: अग्नयः च शान्ताः जज्वलुः। दिग्जनितस्वनाः शान्ताः (अभवन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: अग्नयः (with शान्ताः) जज्वलुः, and दिग्जनितस्वनाः शान्ताः with the verb ‘were’ understood.
mantras.lit: And the fires blazed, calm; stilled (were) the sounds arisen in the quarters.
mantras.tr: The fires blazed up, steady and calm, and the noises that had sounded from every quarter fell still.
mantras.tr_note: The first शान्ताः is rendered ‘steady and calm’; ‘were’ is supplied in the second clause.

comm.t: The last half-śloka of the chapter completes the restoration: fire and sound, which had been disturbed, return to their proper state. The first शान्ताः can also be read ‘(the fires) that had been put out (blazed again)’ — on either reading the fires are restored. This half-line is the one ‘half-śloka’ of the chapter’s colophon count (27 ślokas and 1 half-śloka).

The fires are traditionally understood as the sacrificial fires. Śumbha had claimed every share of the sacrifice for himself (5.108, यज्ञभागानहं सर्वानुपाश्नामि); with him gone, the fires burn again for the gods. The verse itself says only ‘the fires’. In recitation the chapter ends with the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa.

flags.uncertain: Interpretation, not reading: the first शान्ताः may describe the fires as calm (steady) or as having been extinguished before they blazed again. The first is taken here.
